value_chain_position: Focused Brazilian copper producer selling copper concentrate with a gold-byproduct credit; not a converter or processor.
cost_curve_verified: Proxy and company agree in direction, but the proxy flatters: our screen reads a 58.6% trailing margin (62nd percentile of an eight-name cohort), while Ero's own reported first-quarter 2026 cash cost of $2.39 a pound (Caraiba $2.79, Tucuma $1.97, release dated 2026-05-04) is ABOVE its own $2.15-to-$2.35 full-year guidance and places the company in the back half of the global copper cost curve - the margin looks first-quartile only because it is struck on a record copper price.
gm_trajectory: Wrong way on a doubling revenue base: gross margin was 39.8% in the first quarter of 2026 ($103.3M on $259.5M) against 44.4% a year earlier ($55.5M on $125.1M) - down about 4.6 percentage points while revenue rose 107%; the 50.9% printed in the fourth quarter of 2025 was lifted by roughly 15,000 ounces of one-off gold-concentrate stockpile sales carrying only a $300-to-$500-an-ounce cost.
bull_thesis:
Ero is a genuinely repaired operator that spent 2022 to 2024 building a mine and is now being paid for it, into the strongest copper price on record. Three things carry the case.

First, the asset base got structurally better. Tucuma reached commercial production in the second quarter of 2025 and now produces at a cash cost of $1.97 a pound against Caraiba's $2.79 (first quarter of 2026). Every tonne Tucuma adds pulls the consolidated cost curve down, and the additional tailings-filtration equipment being installed this year - deliberately excluded from 2026 guidance, with management describing a one-to-two-quarter payback at current prices - adds throughput on top. The new shaft at Caraiba's Pilar mine, past peak spend and due in 2027, replaces an hour-long ramp drive with a five-minute hoist and should do the same for the higher-cost half of the portfolio.

Second, the operating turnaround is evidenced, not asserted. October 2025 produced all-time monthly records at all three mines, some of them beating marks set many years earlier; the fourth quarter delivered record mill throughput of nearly 1.2 million tonnes at Caraiba and a 22% quarter-on-quarter production increase at Tucuma. Xavantina was fully mechanised ahead of schedule, cutting mining unit costs roughly 30% in local currency, and management turned a decade-old waste stockpile into a 29,000-ounce inferred gold resource sold at a $300-to-$500-an-ounce cost. That is operating creativity, not promotion.

Third, the growth leg is real and cheap to hold. The maiden economic study on the Furnas copper-gold project, published 2026-02-23 - early against a repeatedly stated first-half-2026 promise - outlines a 24-year mine producing roughly 70,000 tonnes of copper, 111,000 ounces of gold and 532,000 ounces of silver a year over its first fifteen years at first-quartile cash costs of about $0.24 a pound, for an after-tax net present value of about $2.0 billion at an 8% discount rate and a 27% internal rate of return on $1.3 billion of initial capital. Ero earns 60% from Vale Base Metals by completing work programmes, and Vale is carried on up to 11% of construction capital. Carrying costs until a construction decision are drilling and studies, not steel.

The financial backdrop supports it. Trailing revenue is $925.2 million, up 89%; trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation are $541.8 million at a 58.6% margin; first-quarter 2026 net income was $108.8 million, or $1.04 a diluted share. Net debt is $490.7 million and leverage is 1.0 times, comfortably inside the 1.5-times target management set in March 2025. Share count rose only about 1.8% over eight quarters - this company funded a mine without shredding its owners. Smelter treatment charges collapsed to roughly minus $70 a tonne by late March 2026, meaning smelters are effectively paying miners to take concentrate, a direct margin tailwind for a pure concentrate seller.

The conditions the case depends on: copper holding near $6 a pound rather than reverting toward the company's own $4.60 planning price; the second half of 2026 delivering the higher grades and throughput that guidance requires, so cash costs fall back inside the $2.15-to-$2.35 range; and Furnas advancing through a pre-feasibility study without an equity call.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Ero is a bad company - it is that the market is paying a full price for peak-cycle earnings at a second-quartile-cost, single-country, levered producer, and the arithmetic of a normal copper price is brutal.

Start with the price. London copper was about $13,799 a tonne, roughly $6.26 a pound, on 2026-07-30, at record levels. Ero's own Furnas study uses a long-term copper price of $4.60 a pound. Today's earnings are struck about 36% above the price the company itself calls normal. At $4.00-to-$4.50 copper, on 2026 guidance of 67,500 to 77,500 tonnes and a realistic $2.20-to-$2.30 cash cost, the whole company generates roughly $300 to $370 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - against guided capital spending of $275 to $320 million and about $33 million of annual interest. Free cash flow goes to approximately zero. That is not a hypothetical: it is what happened. Capital spending of $296 million, $461 million and $338 million in 2022, 2023 and 2024 produced free cash flow of minus $152 million, minus $298 million and minus $192 million, funded with $338 million of new debt in 2022, $104 million of equity in 2023 and $159 million more debt in 2024, plus $160 million of gold-stream proceeds from Royal Gold. The balance sheet still carries $490.7 million of net debt from that programme.

Second, the cost story is already breaking. First-quarter 2026 consolidated cash cost came in at $2.39 a pound, above the $2.15-to-$2.35 guidance, and management guided the second quarter to be "broadly similar to Q1" at Caraiba. The entire year now depends on a second-half grade and throughput recovery. Gross margin fell about 4.6 percentage points year on year while revenue doubled. Brazilian cost inflation was conceded on the November 2025 call, and the currency collars that cushioned it - $240 million notional, floor 5.53 and ceiling 6.52 reais to the dollar - ran only through June 2026, with no disclosed replacement in these materials.

Third, the gold leg has already turned. On the March 2026 call management named byproduct gold as "a big tailwind." Gold is now $4,157.50 an ounce against a fifty-two-week high of $5,626.80 - down about 26% - and Xavantina's first-quarter all-in sustaining cost of $4,441 an ounce sat above the gold price. That hits three lines at once: Xavantina's economics, the remaining concentrate stockpile, and the gold credit that keeps Caraiba's copper cash cost from looking worse than $2.79.

Fourth, the growth asset is also a liability. Furnas needs $1.3 billion of initial capital against a $3.0 billion market value and $491 million of net debt, and about 60% of the material in the study is inferred - the lowest-confidence resource category, not yet usable in a mine plan, as management conceded to CIBC in March 2026. A study-stage project with 60% inferred material and no funding plan is an option, not an asset, and if copper falls the option loses value precisely when the balance sheet needs it most.

Fifth, reserve life is adequate, not long, and the good years are being taken now. Tucuma's published reserve of about 43.1 million tonnes at 0.83% copper was framed as a 12-year life at just over 27,000 tonnes a year; the 2026 run rate is nearer 36,000 tonnes, implying about a decade. Management has said repeatedly that early grades run "2.5 times to 3 times above the life of mine average feed." Caraiba's reserve supports roughly 20 years, but at rising depth and cost until the shaft lands in 2027.

What would confirm the bear case: a second-quarter 2026 cash cost again above $2.35 a pound with 2026 guidance reaffirmed anyway; copper below $5.00 a pound with net debt flat or rising; disclosure of 2026 copper collars that cap the current price; or any equity-linked financing tied to Furnas.

The symmetry matters and it is not decorative. The measured torque of this business is that a 10% move in the metal swings earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation by about 14.5%, or roughly $79 million on the trailing base and closer to $100 million on a spot run-rate base. That is the number the bull quotes on the way up. It is exactly the number that applies on the way down.
sop_bull:
Favourable sum-of-the-parts (valuing each mine separately, then adding the growth asset and subtracting debt) - about $42 a share, assuming copper holds near $6.25 a pound, gold near $4,150 an ounce, the Tucuma filtration expansion lands, and Furnas advances toward a pre-feasibility study. On 105.0 million diluted shares:
- Caraiba (about 36,000 tonnes of copper a year, roughly 20-year reserve life, cash cost about $2.60 a pound): earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of about $290 million at 5.5 times = $1,594 million.
- Tucuma (lifted to about 40,000 tonnes on the new tailings filtration, cash cost about $1.90 a pound, roughly 10-to-12-year reserve life): about $384 million at 6.5 times = $2,494 million.
- Xavantina gold (45,000 ounces, cash cost about $1,125 an ounce, Royal Gold stream in place): about $136 million at 4.0 times = $545 million.
- Head-office costs of about $60 million a year capitalised at 6.0 times = minus $360 million.
- Furnas: Ero's 60% of the study's $2.0 billion after-tax net present value, carried at 40% of that value to reflect a de-risked, better-drilled project = $480 million.
- Net debt falling to about $250 million by end-2027 on sustained spot cash flow = minus $250 million.
Total about $4,503 million, or $42.89 a share; call it $42.
sop_bear:
Adverse sum-of-the-parts - about $12.50 a share, assuming the copper cycle turns against Ero: copper back to $4.00 a pound and gold to $3,000 an ounce, with a weaker Brazilian real cushioning unit costs to about $2.20 a pound consolidated (the natural hedge that partly offsets a metal fall in a Brazilian-cost producer). On 105.0 million diluted shares:
- Caraiba: about $123 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at 4.5 times = $554 million.
- Tucuma: about $173 million at 5.0 times = $865 million.
- Xavantina gold at $3,000 an ounce: about $90 million at 3.5 times = $315 million.
- Head-office costs capitalised at 5.0 times = minus $300 million.
- Furnas carried at only 8% of Ero's 60% share, because a $1.3 billion build is unfinanceable for this balance sheet at $4.00 copper = $96 million.
- Net debt rising to about $560 million as free cash flow goes to zero against $275-to-$320 million of committed capital spending = minus $560 million.
That stack sums to roughly $970 million, or $9.24 a share. Cross-checked against the fifty-two-week low of $13.37, which was struck a year ago at $4.36 copper on materially lower production, the honest adverse level is a little higher than the raw stack: $12.50 a share. Consolidated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in this world are roughly $326 million, against about $542 million trailing - the 14.5% earnings swing per 10% metal move, applied in the direction nobody quotes.
sop_fair_value: $25.75 per share (base case, U.S. dollars, New York listing) - below the $28.76 market price.
sop_breakdown:
Base case assumes copper at $5.25 a pound - above the company's own $4.60 long-term planning price, reflecting genuinely tight concentrate markets and negative smelter treatment charges, but well below the $6.26 record spot - and gold at $3,600 an ounce, on 2026 guidance of 72,500 tonnes of copper and 45,000 ounces of gold. On 105.0 million diluted shares:
- Caraiba Operations: 79.4 million pounds at a $2.65-a-pound margin = about $210 million of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, at 5.5 times = $1,157 million. Roughly 20-year reserve life; the higher-cost half of the portfolio until the Pilar shaft lands in 2027.
- Tucuma Operation: 80.5 million pounds at a $3.30-a-pound margin = about $266 million, at 6.0 times = $1,594 million. The lowest-cost asset and the reason the consolidated cost curve is improving; about a decade of reserve at current rates.
- Xavantina gold: 45,000 ounces at a $2,475-an-ounce margin = about $111 million, at 4.0 times = $446 million. A shorter-life, higher-cost asset carrying a Royal Gold stream against which $160 million of proceeds have already been drawn.
- Head-office costs: about $60 million a year capitalised at 6.0 times = minus $360 million.
- Furnas growth project: Ero's 60% of the study's $2.0 billion after-tax net present value is $1.2 billion, carried at 30% to reflect that about 60% of the study material is inferred, no construction decision exists, and $1.3 billion of initial capital is unfunded = $360 million.
- Net debt: minus $491 million, the company-reported figure at 2026-03-31 (our own recomputation including capitalised leases is $514 million; the $23 million gap is a lease-definition difference and does not change the conclusion).
Total about $2,706 million, or $25.77 a share. The market price of $28.76 therefore embeds a long-run copper price closer to $5.60 to $5.80 a pound - a good outcome already paid for.
risk_reward: From the $28.76 market price: the adverse case sits at $12.50 a share, the base case at $25.75, the favourable case at $42.00. The base case is BELOW the current price - there is no margin of safety at today's level - while the adverse case is a long way down. The asymmetry currently points the wrong way, and it only inverts if copper holds at or above roughly $5.80 a pound indefinitely.
catalyst_status_note: The two load-bearing re-rating events have already happened. Commercial production at Tucuma was declared in the second quarter of 2025, and the maiden economic study on Furnas was published 2026-02-23 (after-tax net present value about $2.0 billion at an 8% discount rate, 27% internal rate of return, 24-year life, $1.3 billion initial capital, first-quartile cash costs of about $0.24 a pound). The shares moved with them - from roughly $27.52 at the end of December 2025 to $32.12 by mid-April 2026 - and have since drifted back to $28.76. What remains ahead is calendar, not thesis: second-quarter 2026 results are scheduled for 2026-08-05 with a call on 2026-08-06 (announced 2026-07-02), a Furnas project update was flagged for mid-2026 with over 75,000 metres drilled through end-May 2026 across ten rigs (release dated 2026-06-10), and a capital markets day is set for mid-September 2026 in Sao Paulo. Under this lane's catalyst-neutrality rule the spent catalyst is neither a penalty nor a credit; the verdict below rests entirely on the residual value case.
peer_comps_note: The relative-value lever gives Ero no discount at all. On enterprise value to trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, Ero trades at 6.6 times against Hudbay Minerals at 6.6 times and Capstone Copper at 6.5 times - the same multiple, for a company with more leverage (net debt of 0.97 times earnings, versus Hudbay in a small net cash position and Capstone at 0.82 times), higher unit cash costs, and every asset in one country. Lundin Mining, First Quantum and Ivanhoe are larger and more diversified across jurisdictions. Ero's offsetting advantages are real - faster near-term volume growth as Tucuma ramps, and the Furnas optionality - but they are advantages the market is already charging for, not discounting. Note also that the entire cohort rose 5% to 8% on 2026-08-04 alongside record copper; this is a sector being marked up together, which is precisely when relative-multiple comfort is least informative.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the operations - it is about what price of copper the share price already assumes.

The street is barely present here. Only four price targets printed in the last twelve months, none in the last quarter, and the newest is 112 days old: $31.00 from Marcio Farid on 2026-04-14, set when the stock was $32.12 - that is, a target roughly 4% BELOW the price at which it was published. Goldman Sachs carried $33.00 on 2026-01-14 with the stock at $29.83. This is not a street-wide view; it is a handful of stale marks that have not been refreshed through a record copper move. Anyone treating the $31.00 consensus as an endorsement is reading a four-month-old note.

The assumption we think is wrong is the implicit one embedded in the price. At $28.76 with $491 million of net debt, the enterprise is valued at about $3.5 billion. Back-solving our own parts stack, that requires a long-run copper price of roughly $5.60 to $5.80 a pound - about 22% to 26% above the $4.60 a pound Ero itself uses to underwrite its flagship growth project, and far above any price the industry sustained before 2025. In other words, the market has already capitalised most of a record spot price as permanent. The debate is not whether copper is tight - concentrate markets genuinely are, with spot smelter treatment charges around minus $70 a tonne by late March 2026, meaning smelters pay miners to take material. The debate is whether a 58.6% trailing margin at a second-quartile-cost producer is an operating achievement or a price artefact. On the company's own reported cash cost of $2.39 a pound - above its own $2.15-to-$2.35 guidance - it is mostly a price artefact.

There is a second, subtler disagreement. Management's March 2026 framing was that Ero is "exiting a major investment cycle... with declining consolidated capital requirements." The company's own 2026 capital guidance of $275 to $320 million is above the $267 million actually spent in 2025. The market has accepted the word "declining"; the guidance says otherwise.

And one disagreement in Ero's favour, for balance: the gold-concentrate stockpile programme and the Xavantina mechanisation are the sort of self-help that almost never appears in a copper-beta model. Both are real and both were delivered. They are worth something - just not the roughly 12% premium to our base-case value that the shares currently carry.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next two to three quarters, and it opens tomorrow.

Second-quarter 2026 results land on 2026-08-05, with the call on 2026-08-06. The setup is uncomfortable: first-quarter cash costs came in at $2.39 a pound against $2.15-to-$2.35 guidance, and management pre-guided that Caraiba's second quarter would be "broadly similar to Q1" before improving in the second half. If the second quarter prints above the range again, the entire year's cost guidance depends on a second-half recovery in grade and throughput - and this is a management team that reaffirmed 2025 guidance twice before cutting it on 2025-08-01, one year to the week earlier. A second reset would cost far more credibility than the first.

The cash mechanics are the real hazard. Capital spending of $275 to $320 million is guided for 2026 against trailing operating cash flow of $396.8 million and trailing free cash flow of only $120.7 million. Add roughly $33 million of annual interest. At today's copper price this is comfortable. At $4.50 a pound it is break-even; at $4.00 a pound free cash flow is approximately zero and net debt starts rising again from $490.7 million. Deleveraging progress in the first quarter was only about $11 million, which tells you how thin the cushion is when a soft quarter meets a heavy capital programme.

Three specific hazards inside the window. First, the currency collars - $240 million notional with a floor of 5.53 and a ceiling of 6.52 reais to the dollar - ran only through June 2026, and no replacement is disclosed in these materials; Brazilian cost inflation was already conceded in November 2025. Second, whether copper hedges exist for 2026 is not disclosed; Ero sold zero-cost collars over 3,000 tonnes a month at a $4.68-a-pound average ceiling in 2025 and gave away the upside, so the question is live and material with copper at $6.26. Third, gold has fallen about 26% from its fifty-two-week high, and Xavantina's first-quarter all-in sustaining cost of $4,441 an ounce already exceeded the gold price - the gold leg is the part of the second-quarter print most likely to disappoint.

The macro backdrop compounds it. The debt cycle currently reads as a discipline phase - positive real long-term rates being imposed and holding, cash flow rewarded and duration punished - which is a poor environment for a story whose largest single asset in the base case is an unfunded, study-stage project needing $1.3 billion. And the commodities-versus-equities dial has actually been falling, down about 19% over three months at the 33rd percentile of its six-year history, even as copper prints records. That divergence usually resolves against the miners, not for them.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling pressure to buy into here, and that cuts both ways.

Ero pays no dividend and has never paid one, so there is no yield-focused shareholder base that a cut could flush out mechanically - the classic washout setup simply does not exist. Shareholders voted through all business at the annual meeting on 2026-06-29 with 82.98% of shares represented; there is no governance fight, no activist, no strategic process, and no premium scenario visible in the record.

The positioning risk runs the other way. The shareholder register is copper-beta money: resource funds, generalists reaching for the metal, and passive flows into a sector that rose 5% to 8% in a single session on 2026-08-04. That base does not liquidate on a dividend cut; it liquidates on the copper chart. Average daily trading is about $9.2 million against a $3.0 billion market value - roughly three-tenths of one percent of the company changing hands per day. That is a thin door for a crowded, momentum-driven register. A sharp copper reversal would meet very little liquidity on the way out, which is why the adverse case in the parts stack looks as violent as it does.

The honest reading of positioning: the marginal buyer today is buying copper exposure, not Ero's cost curve. When that flow reverses, the fact that Tucuma is a good mine will not slow the exit.
forcing_function:
Three dated events, none of which we think forces an upward re-rating from here.

1. Second-quarter 2026 results on 2026-08-05, with the call on 2026-08-06 (announced 2026-07-02). This is the only genuinely binding date in the near term, and it is a test rather than a prize: does the consolidated cash cost come back inside $2.15 to $2.35 a pound, does net debt fall meaningfully below $490.7 million on record realised prices, and are there copper hedges capping the upside? A clean print on all three would be the single best argument against our caution.

2. A Furnas project update flagged for mid-2026, following the 2026-06-10 release confirming high-grade continuity and step-out extensions with over 75,000 metres drilled through end-May and ten rigs turning. The number that matters is not the intercepts; it is how much of the roughly 60% inferred material converts to measured and indicated - the categories that can actually enter a mine plan - ahead of a pre-feasibility study.

3. A capital markets day in mid-September 2026 in Sao Paulo. This is the natural venue for step four of the four-step strategy - the shareholder return promised on every call since March 2025 and deferred every time. A dividend or buyback initiation would be a real signal, though initiating returns at a record copper price while guiding capital spending up would itself be a capital-allocation question, not an answer.

What would genuinely force a re-rating in our direction is none of these: it is a copper price that holds above $6 a pound into 2027 while cash costs fall back inside guidance and net debt drops below $350 million. That is a price event with an operating confirmation, not a corporate event - which is precisely why we would rather wait for a level than for a date.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a better company than it was eighteen months ago and a worse investment than it was six months ago, and both statements rest on the same fact: the copper price.

What we verified is genuinely good. Tucuma works and is the low-cost asset at $1.97 a pound against Caraiba's $2.79. Xavantina was mechanised ahead of plan for roughly a 30% cut in mining unit costs, and a decade-old waste stockpile was engineered into 29,000 ounces of gold sold at a $300-to-$500-an-ounce cost. The Furnas study landed early, on 2026-02-23, and reads well: a 24-year mine at first-quartile costs with an after-tax net present value of about $2.0 billion. Net debt is $490.7 million at 1.0 times earnings, inside the target management set. Share count rose about 1.8% over eight quarters - this management funded a mine build without shredding its owners, which in this sector is worth saying out loud. On the two behaviours that most often destroy mining shareholders - serial equity issuance and buybacks at the top - Ero is clean.

But the three tests this lane actually cares about come out mixed to poor at today's price.

On cost-curve position: the proxy says a 58.6% margin at the 62nd percentile of its cohort; the company says $2.39 a pound in the first quarter of 2026, above its own $2.15-to-$2.35 guidance. When the proxy and the company disagree, the company's unit cost wins, and it says back half of the global cost curve. The margin is flattered by a record metal price, not earned by a privileged orebody.

On contracting and reserve life: adequate, not comfortable, and thinner on disclosure than we would like. Caraiba supports roughly 20 years; Tucuma's 43.1 million tonnes at 0.83% copper implies about a decade at the current 36,000-tonne run rate, against a 12-year framing at 27,000 tonnes - and management has said repeatedly that early grades run two-and-a-half to three times the life-of-mine average, so the good years are being taken now. No concentrate offtake counterparty is named in any of the five calls or in the public releases we checked; management called the terms "long-term contracts that are commercially sensitive." The named counterparties that do exist are high quality - Vale Base Metals at Furnas, Royal Gold on the Xavantina stream - but a pure concentrate seller that will not name a smelter customer is a disclosure gap, and we record it as such rather than assume the worst.

On capital discipline: honourable intent, uncomfortable arithmetic. Ero never bought back stock at the top and never paid a dividend it had to cut - but it did commit heavily through the last cycle, spending $296 million, $461 million and $338 million in 2022 to 2024 for free cash flow of minus $152 million, minus $298 million and minus $192 million, funded with debt, one $104 million equity issue and $160 million of gold-stream proceeds. Crucially, that money bought Tucuma, which works - this is the good version of peak-cycle spending. The uncomfortable part is that 2026 capital guidance of $275 to $320 million is HIGHER than the $267 million spent in 2025, while the March 2026 narrative describes capital requirements as "declining." Step four of the four-step strategy - returns to shareholders - has now been deferred on five consecutive calls.

The regime read is neutral for copper mining, and the wider macro is a discipline phase in which positive real rates are being imposed and cash flow is rewarded over duration - a poor setting for a base case whose second-largest component is an unfunded, study-stage project. Note too that the commodities-versus-equities dial has been falling, down about 19% over three months, even while copper prints records.

The torque cuts both ways and we have priced it that way. A 10% move in the metal swings earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation by about 14.5% - roughly $79 million on the trailing base, closer to $100 million at a spot run rate. Our adverse case does not assume a catastrophe; it assumes copper at $4.00 a pound and gold at $3,000, with a weaker Brazilian real cushioning unit costs, and it still lands at $12.50 a share, because free cash flow goes to zero against $275-to-$320 million of committed capital spending and net debt starts climbing again.

Reconciling the two sides gives a base-case value of about $25.75 a share against a market price of $28.76. There is no margin of safety at this level - the market is already paying for a long-run copper price of roughly $5.60 to $5.80 a pound, well above the $4.60 the company itself uses to underwrite Furnas. The peer check confirms it: at 6.6 times trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, Ero trades at exactly Hudbay's and Capstone's multiple while carrying more debt, higher unit costs and single-country concentration.

So: wait for the wash-out, and here is the specific level. We would be buyers around $20 a share - a genuine discount to our base case, and roughly where a copper pullback toward $5.00 a pound would put the stock - or on evidence rather than price: a second-quarter or third-quarter print that brings the consolidated cash cost back inside $2.15 to $2.35 a pound with net debt below $400 million and no copper collars capping the upside. Either would let us own a repaired operator at a price that does not assume the best copper market in history is permanent. Judged purely on value - price against our reconciled parts value, plus the quality of the forensic record - the shares sit at a premium to fair value with a clean-but-not-pristine record behind them, which is why the value score sits below the execution stance.
